clue_1: He grew up in regional Queensland before his family moved south to Sydney, where as a teenager doubts followed him about whether his slight frame could survive the weekly punishment of the position he would one day come to define
clue_2: Standing only around 173 centimetres, he was unusually short for an elite playmaker, and his mop of blond hair made him instantly recognisable as the on-field general who ran one of the most feared attacking sides of his generation through his passing and pinpoint kicking
clue_3: He twice won the Rothmans Medal as the best player in the Sydney premiership, in 1987 and 1990, an award then widely regarded as the game's highest individual honour for a club footballer
clue_4: He spent his entire first-grade career at a single western-Sydney club, winning premierships in 1981, 1982, 1983 and 1986, his almost telepathic halves partnership with Brett Kenny the engine of those championship teams
clue_5: A chronic shoulder injury forced his retirement in 1992, after which he became one of rugby league's best-known television commentators and analysts, his weekly segment a fixture of Australian football coverage for three decades
clue_6: Parramatta Eels halfback nicknamed 'Sterlo' (1978-1992), four-time premiership winner, dual Rothmans Medallist, member of the club's Team of the Century and a long-serving Channel Nine commentator
facts: The Kangaroo touring sides he played in during 1982 and 1986 both went through their entire tours of Great Britain and France without losing a single match, the 1982 team becoming immortalised as 'The Invincibles'.
Although he was born in Toowoomba in Queensland, he played his State of Origin football for New South Wales, lining up 13 times for the Blues.

During the Australian off-seasons he played in the English competition for Hull, and was widely judged the best player on the field in the famous 1985 Challenge Cup final at Wembley even though his side lost the match.

clue_1: He was born in 1970 in a small country town in Queensland's South Burnett region, one of a large family, and was identified early as one of the most naturally gifted outside backs the state had ever produced
clue_2: Blessed with a gliding running style and a devastating change of pace, he built an elite career despite being diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at the age of 23, managing his blood sugar carefully throughout his playing days
clue_3: He scored 142 tries in 183 first-grade games for his club, a try-scoring record there that has stood for decades, his elusive sidestep making him one of the most feared finishers of his era
clue_4: He won four premierships with the Brisbane Broncos, in 1992, 1993, 1997 and 1998, crossing in deciders alongside teammates such as Allan Langer and the Walters brothers
clue_5: In 2000 he moved to England to finish his career with Wigan, scoring 43 tries in two seasons and earning selection in the competition's dream team before retiring in 2002
clue_6: Brisbane Broncos centre nicknamed 'The Pearl' (1989-1999), four-time premiership winner, the club's record try-scorer and a proud Aboriginal man who became a prominent diabetes and Indigenous-health advocate
facts: He made his Test debut for Australia in front of what was then a world-record rugby league crowd of 73,631, scoring the only try of the match after a pass from his Broncos teammate Kevin Walters.
His nickname 'The Pearl' became so synonymous with him that his 2006 autobiography was titled simply 'The Pearl: Steve Renouf's Story'.
In 2008 he was named at centre in the Indigenous Australian Rugby League Team of the Century, recognised among the greatest Aboriginal players the game has produced.

clue_1: Born in 1989 in a North Queensland sugar town, he was a small, slightly-built outside back whose dazzling footwork made him one of the most exciting young talents of his generation, though a turbulent personal life would repeatedly threaten to derail his career
clue_2: An electric, unpredictable fullback with a low centre of gravity and a devastating step, he became as well known for the personal struggles that shadowed his career as for his brilliance with the ball in hand
clue_3: In 2012 he was awarded the Dally M Medal as the best player in the competition, scoring 21 tries in a single season and being regarded as the most damaging attacking player in the game that year
clue_4: He starred in the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs side that reached the 2012 grand final, then four years later was the running fullback in Cronulla's drought-breaking 2016 premiership, the first in the Sharks' history
clue_5: Days after that premiership a positive drug test ended his time at the club, and after a stint in the English Super League — where he won the 2018 Man of Steel award — his attempted NRL comeback collapsed when he was deregistered indefinitely in early 2019 following a domestic-violence allegation
clue_6: Mackay-born fullback (2008-2019) who won the 2012 Dally M Medal with the Bulldogs and the 2016 premiership with Cronulla, before his NRL career ended in deregistration and he continued playing in lower-grade and overseas competitions
facts: Of Aboriginal and South Sea Islander heritage, he came through the junior ranks in Mackay before the Bulldogs signed him as a teenager.
During a period when he was unable to play in the NRL he briefly switched codes to rugby union, signing with French club Toulon in 2017.
Long after his deregistration he kept playing the game at lower levels in country and second-tier competitions, and as recently as 2025 was reported to be joining another club to extend his career.

clue_1: He was born in 1979 in a coastal village in Fiji before his family emigrated to Australia, where his rare blend of size, speed and aerial ability marked him out as a potential star in more than one football code
clue_2: A towering, powerful winger and centre, he became one of only a handful of men to represent Australia in both rugby league and rugby union, switching codes at the very height of his powers
clue_3: He scored a try in a grand-final-winning side early in his first rugby league stint, and after changing codes he scored one of the most memorable tries in a Rugby World Cup final
clue_4: He won the 2000 NRL premiership on the wing for the Brisbane Broncos, then in 2003 crossed to rugby union and scored in the World Cup final for the Wallabies against England in their extra-time defeat
clue_5: He returned to rugby league in 2010 after seven years away, signing with the Wests Tigers and later moving to South Sydney, completing a rare two-code career that also included representing Fiji
clue_6: Fijian-born winger and centre, a dual-code international who won the 2000 NRL grand final with the Brisbane Broncos, played rugby union for the Wallabies including the 2003 World Cup final, then returned to the NRL with the Wests Tigers and South Sydney
facts: His try in the 2003 Rugby World Cup final helped drag the match into extra time, where England's Jonny Wilkinson landed the drop goal that won the trophy.
In rugby union he played Super Rugby for the New South Wales Waratahs and later joined English club Leicester Tigers before returning to rugby league.
His switch from league to union in 2003 was a high-profile coup for rugby union and one of the era's most talked-about defections between the two rival codes.

clue_1: Born in a remote Western Australian mining town in 1998 to New Zealand parents, he moved as a child first to outback Queensland and then across the Tasman, growing up playing a string of different sports before rugby league finally claimed him
clue_2: An explosive, improvising fullback with a reliable goal-kicking boot and a habit of conjuring something from nothing, he is celebrated equally for spectacular individual tries and for the calm with which he steers a side around the park
clue_3: In 2023 he was awarded the Dally M Medal as the player of the year, and has been named the competition's best fullback on multiple occasions
clue_4: He captains the Newcastle Knights, the club he joined as a teenager from the North Queensland system, and burst into State of Origin in 2018 with a dazzling cameo off the bench for Queensland
clue_5: Troubled at times by concussion problems, he flirted with a move to rugby union and even agreed a deal with New Zealand Rugby before reversing course to commit his long-term future to his NRL club
clue_6: Newcastle Knights captain and fullback (2018-present), the 2023 Dally M Medallist and a Queensland State of Origin fullback, born in Western Australia and raised partly in New Zealand
facts: He was born in Port Hedland in Western Australia, spent part of his childhood in Mount Isa, and lived for five years in Palmerston North, New Zealand, where he played golf, hockey, rugby union and soccer as a boy.
He is of Maori descent through his New Zealand-born father.
He is a genuinely accomplished golfer who has played off a low handicap and has repeatedly named professional golf as the career he might have pursued had rugby league not worked out.
